topic: The Roots of Unity Filter: Harmonic Counting with Generating Functions
target_audience: Advanced high school students (Math Olympiad) and undergraduate mathematics students

sections.title: Prerequisite: The DNA of Combinatorics
sections.content: Introduce the Generating Function (GF) as a 'container' for sequences. Explain that a polynomial like (1+x)^n stores the number of ways to choose 'k' items in the coefficient of x^k. Use a visual of a conveyor belt where boxes (coefficients) represent the number of ways to pick items.
sections.example: If we have 3 distinct apples, (1+x)^3 = 1 + 3x + 3x^2 + 1x^3. The coefficient '3' for x^2 means there are 3 ways to pick exactly 2 apples.

sections.title: The 'Divisibility' Challenge
sections.content: Define the problem: What if we only want the sum of every k-th coefficient? For example, the sum of ways to choose a subset whose size is a multiple of 3. Visually represent this as a 'Sieve' that only lets through the 0th, 3rd, 6th... terms of the polynomial.
sections.example: In a group of 10 friends, how many ways can we form a sub-committee whose size is a multiple of 4 (size 0, 4, or 8)?

sections.title: The Tool: Roots of Unity & The Circle of Cancellation
sections.content: Introduce complex numbers on the unit circle. Explain the property of 'ω' (the n-th root of unity). Show visually that the sum of powers of ω equals 'n' if the index is a multiple of n, and '0' otherwise. Use a 'Clock' animation where vectors either cancel each other out or line up perfectly to create a surge.
sections.example: For n=3, the three vectors (1, ω, ω²) are 120 degrees apart. Summing them yields zero—a perfect balance. But summing their 3rd powers (1³, 1³, 1³) yields 3.

sections.title: The Roots of Unity Filter Formula
sections.content: Combine the Generating Function P(x) with the Roots of Unity. Explain the formula: Sum = [P(ω^0) + P(ω^1) + ... + P(ω^{k-1})] / k. This is the 'Filter' that extracts specific coefficients. Show an animation of plugging different points on the complex circle into the polynomial and averaging the results.
sections.example: To find the sum of coefficients a_0 + a_4 + a_8... of P(x), we calculate [P(1) + P(i) + P(-1) + P(-i)] / 4.

sections.title: Application: The Robot Selection Protocol
sections.content: Apply the concept to a concrete scenario. A factory has 100 robots. They need to select a task force, but the power grid only supports squads of size 0, 4, 8... up to 100. Use the formula derived in Section 4 to show how a seemingly impossible sum (combinations of 100 choose 0, 4, 8...) collapses into a simple calculation using complex numbers.
sections.example: Calculate [(1+1)^100 + (1+i)^100 + (1-1)^100 + (1-i)^100] / 4. Show how (1+i)^100 simplifies via polar coordinates to a real number, revealing the final count instantly.
